svg.aria-label: Sanger dideoxy sequencing with chain termination and capillary separation compared with next generation sequencing by library preparation, cluster amplification and sequencing by synthesis
svg.text: Two ways to read a DNA sequence
A. Sanger (dideoxy) sequencing
ddNTP lacks the 3' hydroxyl, so the chain stops where it is incorporated.
Added in small amounts, so each chain stops at a different position.
each ddNTP carries its own
fluorescent colour
fragments differ by one
nucleotide in length
capillary electrophoresis separates by length; reading the colours in order gives the sequence
700-1000 bp per read, very accurate, one region per reaction
B. Next-generation sequencing
1. Library preparation
fragment DNA to a few hundred bp, add adapters at both ends
2. Cluster amplification
fix each fragment to a spot on a surface and amplify it in place
3. Sequencing by synthesis
add one labelled nucleotide at a time and image the whole surface;
hundreds of millions of spots are read in parallel
4. Align short reads to a reference, or assemble them by overlap
Comparison and applications
Sanger: 700-1000 bp, kb per run, highest accuracy; confirming a single variant
Short-read NGS: 100-300 bp, hundreds of Gb per run; whole genome and transcriptome
Long-read NGS: 10-100 kb; repeat regions and structural variants
Built on NGS: whole genome sequencing, exome sequencing, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, single-cell RNA-seq. The Human Genome Project needed 13 years with Sanger chemistry.
